what_it_does: When a chip is being designed, engineers sometimes need to move cells (the tiny logical building blocks, like gates and flip-flops) around on the layout even late in the process — these last-minute tweaks are called Engineering Change Orders, or ECOs. Every time a cell moves, the electrical resistance and inductance of the power delivery network change slightly, causing voltage fluctuations across the chip called IR-drop (named after Ohm's law: voltage drop equals current times resistance). If the voltage drops too far, transistors slow down or fail. Checking whether a proposed ECO causes a dangerous IR-drop normally requires running a detailed electrical simulation (called a SPICE simulation) that can take over an hour per candidate change. This paper trains an XGBoost machine-learning model — a fast, tree-based prediction algorithm — to estimate the IR-drop for a moved cell in minutes, without any simulation, by looking at the broader neighborhood of cells around it. This lets designers evaluate many ECO candidates in parallel during a single design iteration, dramatically speeding up the sign-off process.
